speaker: Gavin Baker
title: GPUs, TPUs, & The Economics of AI Explained | Gavin Baker Interview
question: In AI infrastructure, why do most hyperscalers' custom ASIC programs struggle to match leading merchant GPUs?
guest: The competitive response of AMD and Nvidia to everybody saying, "We're going to have our own ASIC," is, "Hey, we're just going to accelerate. We're going to do a GPU every year, and you cannot keep up with us." And then what everybody is learning is, "Oh wow, that's so cool, you made your own accelerator as an ASIC. What's the NIC going to be? What's the CPU going to be? What's the scale-up switch going to be? What's the scale-up protocol? What's the scale-out switch? What kind of optics are you going to use? What's the software that's going to make all this work together?" And it also takes at least three generations to make a good chip. Like the TPU v1, it was an achievement in that they made it, but it was really not until TPU v3 or v4 that the TPU started to become even vaguely competitive.

points.core: Merchant GPU leaders accelerate to an annual release cadence competitors cannot match.
points.note: Accept: yearly GPU architecture cadence outpacing internal ASIC roadmaps. Do not credit: vague claims that Nvidia innovates fast without citing the annual release cadence.

points.core: Building an accelerator chip solves only one piece of full-stack system integration.
points.note: Accept: needing NICs, CPUs, scale-up/scale-out switches, optics, or unified software around the ASIC die. Do not credit: generic mentions of 'CUDA moat' without the broader rack and networking stack.

points.core: Developing a competitive custom chip requires at least three generations of iteration.
points.note: Accept: multi-generation learning-by-doing curve (typically 3-4 generations, e.g., TPU v3/v4 or Trainium 3/4) before parity. Do not credit: generic claims that hardware takes time without a multi-generation learning curve.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Most hyperscaler ASIC programs fall short because matching a merchant GPU means matching an entire platform, not just a chip.

The biggest gap is software. Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem has nearly two decades of libraries, compilers, framework optimizations and developer familiarity behind it, so new models run well on GPUs from day one. Custom silicon needs its own stack, and porting and tuning workloads costs engineering time that often erases the hardware savings.

Timing is the second problem. An ASIC takes two to three years to design, so its architecture is locked around assumptions about workloads that may have shifted by the time it ships. Meanwhile, Nvidia now updates its line annually, funded by R&D spending that is amortized over the whole market, whereas a single hyperscaler's volume is far smaller.

Third, performance is increasingly decided at the system level: networking, interconnects, memory, packaging and rack-scale integration. Merchant vendors co-design all of these and have priority access to scarce leading-edge wafers, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory.

ASICs therefore succeed mainly on narrow, stable, high-volume internal workloads, especially inference. Google's TPU is the notable exception, after roughly a decade of iteration.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Most hyperscaler custom ASIC programs struggle to match leading merchant GPUs because frontier AI performance depends on full-stack co-design, software maturity, and scale economics rather than chip logic alone. Custom silicon takes two to three years from specification to deployment, yet AI architectures, numerical precisions, and inference paradigms shift constantly; narrower designs risk partial obsolescence before tape-out, whereas programmable GPUs adapt readily and ship on aggressive annual cadences. Even when custom chips offer competitive peak compute, immature compilers, debugging friction, and gaps in operator coverage often bottleneck real-world utilization, falling short of the deep optimization across CUDA, PyTorch, and collective communication libraries built over nearly two decades. Moreover, modern AI operates as a rack-scale distributed system requiring ultra-fast chip interconnects, scale-out networking, and priority allocation of scarce high-bandwidth memory and advanced foundry packaging. Finally, merchant GPU vendors amortize tens of billions of dollars in R&D across the entire global market, while hyperscalers must justify comparable investments against narrower internal workloads, a hurdle few outside Google's long-running TPU program have cleared.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Most hyperscaler ASIC programs fall short because Nvidia's lead is about the whole system, and the chip is only one part of it. Merchant GPUs come with CUDA and nearly two decades of tuned libraries, compilers and framework support. A custom chip needs its own software stack, and until that stack matures, real-world utilization stays well below the chip's theoretical peak.

Nvidia also releases a new generation every year. A custom ASIC usually takes two to three years to design and is locked to the workloads its designers expected, so it can be out of date by launch, especially as model architectures shift from CNNs to transformers, MoE and long-context inference.

Scale matters too. Nvidia gets first claim on TSMC's leading-edge nodes, CoWoS packaging and HBM, and it adds NVLink networking and complete rack designs. Hyperscalers rarely match that volume or co-design depth.

Google's TPU is the main exception, because it has run for about ten years with its software and models built together. Most other programs win only on cost per unit of work for narrow internal tasks, not on absolute performance or flexibility.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Most hyperscaler custom AI ASICs struggle to match leading merchant GPUs because the real bottleneck is rarely raw silicon compute—it is software, systems engineering, and cadence. Leading merchant GPUs rest on decades of software investment, including CUDA, hand-tuned kernels, and collective communication libraries, which deliver high real-world utilization across frameworks like PyTorch. Building an equivalent compiler and runtime stack from scratch takes years, often leaving strong theoretical hardware underutilized and costly for ML teams to adopt.

Meanwhile, ASICs require multi-year design cycles that lock in architectural bets on precision formats, memory ratios, and communication patterns. Because frontier AI workloads evolve rapidly—shifting toward mixture-of-experts, long-context attention, and low-precision inference—custom silicon frequently arrives optimized for yesterday's models, while GPUs retain greater flexibility. Finally, merchant leaders amortize massive R&D across the entire market to sustain an annual release cadence, secure advanced packaging and HBM supply, and co-design rack-scale interconnects that few hyperscalers, beyond mature programs like Google's TPUs, can match.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Most hyperscalers can design an ASIC that beats a merchant GPU on a specific workload. The harder part is matching the GPU across changing models and getting comparable performance from an entire cluster. Leading GPU vendors invest across the stack, from high-bandwidth memory and interconnects to compilers, optimized kernels, and distributed training libraries. That software and networking help keep thousands of chips busy, so peak chip performance alone tells you little about the cost of training a model or serving a token.

Merchant vendors also spread those investments across many customers and workloads. A hyperscaler has to justify its design costs with its own volume and commit to hardware years ahead of deployment, while model architectures, numerical formats, and memory needs can shift much faster. Custom ASICs are most competitive when the operator has enough predictable demand and the engineering depth to optimize the whole stack. Google’s TPU program is a prominent example.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A custom ASIC can beat a leading merchant GPU on cost or energy per token for a workload it was designed to run. The harder task is sustaining that advantage across different models and thousands of chips. Peak arithmetic throughput matters little if processors spend much of their time waiting for data from memory or for results from other chips.

Leading GPU vendors have spent years tuning memory systems, interconnects, compilers, and software libraries together. They also spread that investment across many customers. A hyperscaler must fund much of that work for its own fleet, persuade teams to port and tune their models, and keep the chips busy enough to recover the upfront cost.

Timing compounds the problem. An ASIC’s design is fixed well before deployment, while model architectures and numerical formats keep evolving. Custom chips therefore tend to be most competitive where demand is large and predictable, such as high-volume inference.
